rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act: criminal-record screening limits
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not put criminal-record questions on an application, or ask about criminal records orally or in writing, before a conditional offer. Two exceptions apply: methamphetamine manufacture on federally assisted premises, and lifetime sex-offender registration. At no stage may a provider evaluate arrests or charges without conviction, expunged convictions, pardoned convictions, vacated convictions, juvenile adjudications or sealed records. After a conditional offer, a provider may consider only: (1) convictions for listed serious crimes or offenses requiring lifetime registration, and (2) indictable offenses within the lookback periods. A conditional offer may be withdrawn only if the provider finds, by a preponderance of the evidence, that withdrawal is necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate and nondiscriminatory interest. The provider must first make an individualized assessment. Withdrawal requires written notice giving specific reasons and an opportunity to appeal. The applicant may request, within 30 days, the information the provider relied on, and the provider must supply it free within 10 days. Before accepting any application fee, the provider must disclose in writing whether criminal history is reviewed and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracy, rehabilitation or mitigation. Discriminatory advertising about criminal records is barred, as is misuse or dissemination of records. Drug or alcohol tests, and consent to obtain drug-treatment information, may not be required. Landlords are immune from civil liability for renting to people with records or for not screening. Enforcement is only through complaints to the Division on Civil Rights, not in court. The Division first offers 14-day mediation. Penalties are capped at $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000 depending on prior violations. The director may also order return of the application fee and payment of up to $1,000 to the applicant.
rules.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before conditional offer; lookback 6 yrs (1st degree), 4 yrs (2nd/3rd degree), 1 yr (4th degree); no limit for murder, aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping, arson, human trafficking, listed sex offenses or lifetime registration; records request within 30 days, provided free within 10 days; penalties up to $1,000 / $5,000 / $10,000

rules.title: Residential rental application fee cap ($50, CPI-adjusted)
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee above $50 to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes. Penalties are up to $500 for a first offense, $750 for a second and $1,000 for each later offense. Penalties are enforced by summary proceedings in the Superior Court, Special Civil Part, on complaint of the Director of Consumer Affairs or the Attorney General. The amount wrongfully charged is paid back to the applicant from the penalty collected. From January 1 of the year after enactment, the cap is adjusted each year by the percent change in CPI-U (New York-Northern New Jersey-Long Island). An adjustment is made only if that change is above zero. The Director publishes the current cap online and must adopt rules, including a way to report violations.
rules.key_value: $50 max application fee (CPI adjustment begins January 1, 2027); penalties up to $500 / $750 / $1,000; overcharge remitted to applicant

rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law
rules.requirement: A landlord may collect a security deposit of no more than 1.5 times one month's rent. Any pet deposit and any prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, count toward this cap. At lease start, the landlord may require at most 2.5 months' rent: the deposit plus first month's rent. A yearly increase may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. The deposit remains the tenant's property and must be held in trust in an interest-bearing account at an insured New Jersey institution, without commingling. Landlords holding deposits for 10 or more units may instead use certain insured money market funds. Interest belongs to the tenant. Within 30 days of receiving the deposit, and with each annual interest payment, the landlord must give written notice of the institution, amount, account type and rate. If notice or interest is not provided, the tenant may have the deposit plus 7% annual interest applied to rent. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the deposit plus interest, less deductions itemized by registered or certified mail. Return is due within 5 business days if the tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation. A tenant may sue for double the amount wrongfully withheld, plus costs and attorney's fees.

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act (good cause eviction)
rules.requirement:
A landlord may not evict a tenant, or refuse to renew a lease, without good cause. The statutory causes are:
- nonpayment of rent
- disorderly conduct
- property damage
- substantial breach of rules or lease covenants
- failure to pay a rent increase that is not unconscionable and complies with local ordinances
- health and safety removal or government redevelopment
- permanent retirement from residential use
- refusal of reasonable lease changes
- habitual late payment
- condominium, cooperative or fee-simple conversion
- owner or buyer occupancy after conversion or in small buildings
- end of employment-based tenancy
- certain drug, assault, theft and human-trafficking offenses

A written Notice to Quit is required for every cause except nonpayment. Some causes also require a prior Notice to Cease, which has no statutory period but must allow reasonable time. Only a court judgment and warrant for removal can remove a tenant, and self-help eviction is illegal. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance of six times monthly rent. Rooming and boarding house owners must follow the same causes and notice rules. They must also give the County Welfare Board 3 working days' notice. Landlords who misuse a unit after an owner-occupancy or retirement eviction face treble damages. Residential reuse within 5 years after a retirement eviction can bring civil penalties up to $10,000.
rules.key_value: Notice to Quit periods: 3 days (disorderly conduct, damage, employment end, criminal offenses); 1 month (rule/lease breach, rent increase, lease changes, habitual late payment); 2 months (post-conversion/small-building owner or buyer occupancy); 3 months (health and safety removal); 18 months (retirement from residential use); 3 years (conversion). Relocation assistance for illegal occupancy: 6x monthly rent.

unverifiable_exemptions: Unit held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member who permanently occupies it
Hotel, motel or guest house rented to a transient or seasonal guest

The Notice to Quit is 3 months for at-will or year-to-year tenancies, 1 month for month-to-month tenancies, and 3 days for disorderly, destructive or rule-violation causes.
coverage.other_conditions: Hotel and motel guests are covered if they have no alternate residence and live there continuously. A landlord who is not properly registered under the landlord registration law cannot obtain an eviction until it complies.

rules.exemptions: Transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest-house guests; units held in trust for a developmentally disabled family member; owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings are subject only to a narrower list of causes.

rules.title: Foreclosure tenant protections and notices (Foreclosure Fairness Act)
rules.requirement: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction. A buyer of a foreclosed property who wants to live in it as a primary residence must give a 90-day notice to quit. A tenant whose lease runs longer than 90 days cannot be evicted until the lease expires. Within 10 business days after the sale, anyone who acquires a foreclosed property with rental units must give tenants a notice in English and Spanish. The notice states that ownership has changed and that tenants need not move. In buildings with more than 10 units, the notice is posted in a prominent location instead. Foreclosing creditors must give the court-rule notice of tenant rights. Any money offer to get tenants to leave must come with a separate notice and a five-day review period. Pressure tactics are barred, including harassment and unconscionable rent increases.
rules.key_value: 90-day notice to quit; tenant notice within 10 business days after sale (English and Spanish); 5-day review period for buyout offers

coverage.summary: Applies to residential rental units in foreclosed properties. Month-to-month tenants and owner-occupied two- and three-family units are not exempt from the 90-day notice. Buildings with more than 10 units use posted notice.
coverage.other_conditions: Triggered only by foreclosure and the sale or transfer of the property.

rules.title: Reprisal protections for tenants
rules.requirement:
A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant by eviction, substantial alteration of the lease or its terms, or refusal to renew. This protection applies when the tenant does any of the following:
- enforces rights under the lease or the law
- makes a good-faith complaint to a government authority, after first notifying the landlord in writing and allowing reasonable time to fix the problem
- organizes or joins a lawful tenant organization
- refuses lease changes made in retaliation

The tenant may sue for damages.

rules.title: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (condominium/cooperative conversion protections)
rules.requirement: When a building is converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership, qualifying tenants may obtain protected tenancy, which protects them from eviction for up to 40 years. Qualifying tenants are those aged 62 or older before the conversion recording date, permanently disabled tenants, or service-disabled veterans rated 60% or higher. They must have lived in the building at least one year before the recording date. Family income must not exceed three times the county average per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater. The landlord or converter must notify tenants of the right to apply. Applications are generally due within 60 days. For all tenants in a converting building, whether protected or not, rents may not be raised to cover costs that result solely from the conversion. Increases for new services or amenities remain allowed.

rules.title: NJ Law Against Discrimination: source of lawful income and other protected characteristics in rental housing
rules.requirement: The Law Against Discrimination bars housing discrimination, including refusal to rent, based on source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment. It also bars discrimination on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital, civil union or domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, disability and nationality. For example, a landlord cannot deny a Section 8 voucher holder an apartment based solely on that source of income. Discriminatory advertising is barred. A landlord may still refuse for insufficient income, an oversized family, an occupancy that would violate zoning, or poor credit history. Complaints may be filed free with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, or in Superior Court within two years. Fines run up to $10,000 for a first offense.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement:
The act makes the following unlawful, each as a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act:
- for a rental property owner or its agent or subcontractor to pay for, subscribe to or contract for a coordinator's services
- for a coordinator to facilitate an agreement among owners that restricts competition, including by performing a coordinating function
- for two or more persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination
- for a coordinator's agents to engage in parallel pricing coordination
- for any person to perform a coordinating function

A coordinating function means algorithmic or automated setting or recommending of rents, material lease terms or occupancy levels that either (1) uses nonpublic, competitively sensitive information of other owners, or (2) applies a common algorithm for two or more owners in a way that facilitates parallel pricing.

Antitrust Act remedies (C.56:9-6 to 9-17) apply. The Attorney General must set up a complaint location and may adopt rules. Municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances.
rules.key_value: Effective July 1, 2027; violations treated as New Jersey Antitrust Act violations; municipal ordinances that conflict with the act are prohibited

coverage.landlord_size_condition: Applies to any rental property owner owning, directly or indirectly, one or more rental residential dwelling units.
coverage.summary: Covers residential dwelling units (houses, apartments, accessory units and other primary residences) in New Jersey. Inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care and detention or correctional facilities are excluded.
coverage.other_conditions: The following are not algorithmic devices: spreadsheets that run without AI and require human analysis, and databases that only query unprocessed data. The following are not coordinating functions: research, statistical or testing uses not used to set rents; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage listing databases that neither set nor recommend rents; and government affordability controls.

rules.exemptions: Non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis; query-only databases; research or testing uses not used for pricing; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage databases; government affordability controls. Residential dwelling unit excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care and detention facilities.
rules.effective_date_note: Approved July 20, 2026, and effective on the first day of the twelfth month after enactment, which is July 1, 2027. The act is not yet effective on the query date.
